claim: B. subtilis grows on surfaces in biofilm or non-biofilm colonies depending on the growth medium.
source: In laboratory conditions, B. subtilis grows on surfaces in biofilm or non-biofilm colonies depending on the growth medium.
evidence: This is stated directly in the text as an established fact about B. subtilis growth behavior.

claim: In LB medium, B. subtilis grows as a colony with limited biofilm characteristics.
source: In the commonly used rich medium lysogeny broth (LB), B. subtilis grows as a colony with limited biofilm characteristics (Shemesh and Chai, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shemesh and Chai, 2013.

claim: When cultured on MSgg medium, B. subtilis natural isolates produce extracellular matrix composed of secreted polysaccharides and proteinaceous components.
source: By contrast, when cultured on the biofilm-promoting minimal medium MSgg (Branda et al., 2001), B. subtilis natural isolates produce extracellular matrix composed of secreted polysaccharides and proteinaceous components that hold cells together and enhance biofilm colony expansion (Kim et al., 2016; Seminara et al., 2012; van Gestel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Extracellular matrix holds cells together and enhances biofilm colony expansion.
source: By contrast, when cultured on the biofilm-promoting minimal medium MSgg (Branda et al., 2001), B. subtilis natural isolates produce extracellular matrix composed of secreted polysaccharides and proteinaceous components that hold cells together and enhance biofilm colony expansion (Kim et al., 2016; Seminara et al., 2012; van Gestel et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Extracellular matrix establishes colony architecture through the three-dimensional pattern of growth and wrinkling.
source: The extracellular matrix also establishes colony architecture through the three-dimensional pattern of growth and wrinkling (Asally et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Asally et al., 2012.

claim: Biofilms contain functionally distinct subpopulations including extracellular matrix producers, sporulating cells, and motile cells.
source: This architecture creates a variety of contexts for genetically identical cells to differentially express genes depending on their location, and indeed biofilms contain functionally distinct subpopulations (López et al., 2010; Vlamakis et al., 2013): living cells differentiate into extracellular matrix producers, sporulating cells, and motile cells, while dead cells may be cannibalized (Blair et al., 2008; Cairns et al., 2014; Vlamakis et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Dead cells in biofilms may be cannibalized.
source: This architecture creates a variety of contexts for genetically identical cells to differentially express genes depending on their location, and indeed biofilms contain functionally distinct subpopulations (López et al., 2010; Vlamakis et al., 2013): living cells differentiate into extracellular matrix producers, sporulating cells, and motile cells, while dead cells may be cannibalized (Blair et al., 2008; Cairns et al., 2014; Vlamakis et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: A library of 302 CRISPRi knockdown strains was constructed in B. subtilis 3610.
source: The library contains 302 strains: the 252 known essential genes in B. subtilis strain 168, 47 genes that were initially classified as essential in 168 (Kobayashi et al., 2003) but later revealed to be non-essential or conditionally essential (Koo et al., 2017), and three internal controls expressing dCas9 without any guide RNAs (Supplementary file 1; Peters et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the library construction performed in this study, with citations to prior work on gene essentiality.

claim: The sacA::gfp strain exhibited similar colony growth and biofilm wrinkling as a parental unlabeled control on both LB and MSgg agar.
source: The sacA::gfp strain exhibited similar colony growth and biofilm wrinkling as a parental unlabeled control on both non-biofilm LB agar and biofilm-promoting MSgg (Branda et al., 2001) agar (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: CRISPRi can be used to knock down gene expression in non-biofilm and biofilm colonies.
source: Thus, CRISPRi is an effective tool to knock down gene expression in non-biofilm and biofilm colonies.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from experimental data showing RFP knockdown in colonies (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).

claim: RFP levels in non-biofilm colonies on LB agar ranged from 40% (basal knockdown) to ~0% (full knockdown).
source: In this strain, RFP levels in non-biofilm colonies on LB agar plates ranged from 40% (basal knockdown) to ~0% (full knockdown) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A), a comparable range to knockdown of the domesticated strain 168 in liquid LB (Peters et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: RFP levels in biofilm colonies on MSgg agar ranged from ~90% (basal knockdown) to ~0% (full knockdown).
source: RFP levels in biofilm colonies on MSgg agar ranged from ~90% (basal knockdown) to ~0% (full knockdown) (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Quantification of the titration row closely agreed with the predicted ratio of GFP:RFP at each time point (16, 24, and 48 hr).
source: Quantification of the titration row closely agreed with the predicted ratio of GFP:RFP at each time point (16, 24, and 48 hr) (Figure 1D, S1B, E), indicating that the relative fraction of GFP-labeled mutants in co-culture with the parent-RFP strain can be accurately quantified through comparison of the GFP:RFP ratio with the titration row (Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: Colony sizes of basal knockdown monocultures exhibited a narrow distribution on LB agar after 16 hr of growth.
source: After 16 hr of growth, colony sizes of basal knockdown monocultures exhibited a narrow distribution on LB agar, but were more widely distributed on MSgg agar (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 2), indicating increased sensitivity to knockdown on MSgg.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures.

claim: Colony sizes of basal knockdown monocultures were more widely distributed on MSgg agar after 16 hr of growth.
source: After 16 hr of growth, colony sizes of basal knockdown monocultures exhibited a narrow distribution on LB agar, but were more widely distributed on MSgg agar (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 2), indicating increased sensitivity to knockdown on MSgg.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A and supplementary figures.

claim: Only 92 of the strains had fitness within two standard deviations of the mean of controls on LB agar after 16 hr under basal knockdown.
source: By contrast to growth as monocultures on LB, basal knockdowns co-cultured with the parent for 16 hr exhibited a broad distribution of competitive fitness on LB agar: only 92 of the strains had a fitness within two standard deviations of the mean of controls, while the remaining 210 strains were significantly defective in competition (below two standard deviations of the mean of the controls) (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary files.

claim: 210 strains were significantly defective in competition on LB agar after 16 hr under basal knockdown.
source: By contrast to growth as monocultures on LB, basal knockdowns co-cultured with the parent for 16 hr exhibited a broad distribution of competitive fitness on LB agar: only 92 of the strains had a fitness within two standard deviations of the mean of controls, while the remaining 210 strains were significantly defective in competition (below two standard deviations of the mean of the controls) (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary files.

claim: 198 basal knockdowns exhibited a significant fitness defect on MSgg agar after 16 hr.
source: On MSgg agar, competitive fitness displayed a similar trend, with 198 basal knockdowns exhibiting a significant fitness defect after 16 hr (Figure 2A, B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, B and supplementary files.

claim: 168 strains had fitness <0.08 after 16 hr of growth on LB xylose agar under full knockdown.
source: As expected, when transcription was fully knocked down, fitness was even more compromised: 168 and 143 strains had fitness <0.08 after 16 hr of growth on LB xylose and MSgg xylose agar, respectively (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary files.

claim: 143 strains had fitness <0.08 after 16 hr of growth on MSgg xylose agar under full knockdown.
source: As expected, when transcription was fully knocked down, fitness was even more compromised: 168 and 143 strains had fitness <0.08 after 16 hr of growth on LB xylose and MSgg xylose agar, respectively (Figure 2B, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B and supplementary files.

claim: Structural constituents of ribosomes were significantly enriched among strains with competitive fitness >2 standard deviations below the mean of controls.
source: Analysis of DAVID functional annotations of strains with competitive fitness >2 standard deviations below the mean of controls revealed significant enrichment of structural constituents of ribosomes (p=9.8 × 10−4 and p=2.1 × 10−2 on LB and MSgg agar, respectively).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of functional annotations using DAVID.

claim: Some ribosomal protein knockdown strains exhibited ~20% lower maximum growth rate than wild type in liquid cultures.
source: Some of the ribosomal protein knockdown strains that competed most poorly exhibited ~20% lower maximum growth rate than wild type in liquid cultures (Figure 2C), suggesting that the reduced competitive fitness of these strains is due to their reduced growth rate.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: A reaction-diffusion model of colony growth indicated that a strain's maximum growth rate is a major determinant of competitive fitness.
source: Indeed, a reaction-diffusion model of colony growth of a co-culture indicated that a strain's maximum growth rate is a major determinant of competitive fitness, and that the 20% decrease of maximum growth rate in certain ribosomal protein knockdowns is consistent with our experimental measurements of their competitive fitness (Figure 2E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1C, Materials and methods).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in figures.

claim: 41 strains on LB and 46 strains on MSgg had fitness similar to controls even at full knockdown.
source: DAVID functional enrichment analysis of basal knockdowns with fitness values within one standard deviation of the mean across controls (n = 41 and 46 strains for LB and MSgg, respectively) highlighted integral membrane components on both solid media (p=2.1 × 10−3 for both LB and MSgg).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Integral membrane components were enriched among basal knockdowns with fitness values within one standard deviation of the mean across controls.
source: DAVID functional enrichment analysis of basal knockdowns with fitness values within one standard deviation of the mean across controls (n = 41 and 46 strains for LB and MSgg, respectively) highlighted integral membrane components on both solid media (p=2.1 × 10−3 for both LB and MSgg).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of functional annotations using DAVID.

claim: Four strains (menH and cytC on LB and aroF and rny on MSgg) had compromised monoculture growth but high competitive fitness under basal knockdown.
source: Under basal knockdown conditions, there were four strains (menH and cytC on LB and aroF and rny on MSgg) in which monoculture growth was clearly compromised by gene knockdown but competitive fitness remained high (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The competitive fitness phenotype was highly reproducible and relatively stable over 2 days of colony growth.
source: We found that the competitive fitness phenotype was highly reproducible and relatively stable over 2 days of colony growth (Figure 2D, E, Figure 2—figure supplement 1D, E), highlighting the utility of our CRISPRi library for probing the fitness of essential gene knockdown in co-cultures.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in multiple figures.

claim: 93% of the strains exhibited similar competitive fitness on MSgg and LB agar under basal or full knockdown.
source: Somewhat surprisingly given the likelihood of different metabolic profiles due to media compositional differences, 93% of the strains exhibited similar competitive fitness (defined here as within 0.24 or 0.3 of the y=x line for basal or full knockdown, respectively) on MSgg and LB agar, whether the targeted gene was basally or fully knocked down (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A and supplementary files.

claim: 36 strains competed with the parent-RFP strain better on MSgg than on LB, or vice versa, under basal or full knockdown.
source: Nonetheless, we identified 36 strains that competed with the parent-RFP strain better on MSgg than on LB, or vice versa, under basal or full knockdown (Figure 3A, B, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A, B and supplementary files.

claim: Strains that competed better in one medium compared to the other were statistically enriched for genes involved in amino acid biosynthesis.
source: Strains that competed better in one medium compared to the other were statistically enriched for genes involved in amino acid biosynthesis (p=4.7×10−6 and p=8.3×10−5 for basal and full knockdown, respectively), suggesting that some strains benefit from nutritional components specific to one medium (Figure 3A, Supplementary file 3).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of functional annotations.

claim: Addition of glycine to MSgg significantly improved fitness of the glyA knockdown in basal and induced conditions.
source: The glyA knockdown had higher competitive fitness on LB agar than on MSgg agar, and as hypothesized, addition of glycine to MSgg significantly improved fitness in basal and induced conditions, to levels close to fitness on LB (Figure 3C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Adding Mg2+ to LB agar restored the competitive fitness of mgtE full knockdowns to levels on MSgg.
source: Similarly, adding Mg2+ or Mn2+ to LB agar at the same levels as in MSgg restored the competitive fitness of mgtE and mntA full knockdowns, respectively, to levels on MSgg (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claim: Adding Mn2+ to LB agar restored the competitive fitness of mntA full knockdowns to levels on MSgg.
source: Similarly, adding Mg2+ or Mn2+ to LB agar at the same levels as in MSgg restored the competitive fitness of mgtE and mntA full knockdowns, respectively, to levels on MSgg (Figure 3C, Figure 3—figure supplement 1A, Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3C and supplementary figures.

claim: alrA was the only knockdown in the thrC::gfp library that failed to form a colony as a monoculture but survived with the parent-RFP strain in biofilm colonies on MSgg agar with xylose.
source: In the thrC::gfp library, alrA was the only knockdown that failed to form a colony as a monoculture but survived with the parent-RFP strain in biofilm colonies on MSgg agar with xylose (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A and supplementary figures.

claim: AlrA is a racemase that converts L-alanine to D-alanine and is required for cross-linking of the peptidoglycan cell wall.
source: AlrA is a racemase that converts L-alanine to D-alanine and is required for cross-linking of the peptidoglycan cell wall (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of AlrA.

claim: Full knockdown of alrA expression during liquid growth led to bulging indicative of cell wall defects.
source: Full knockdown of alrA expression during liquid growth in a strain without gfp disruption of thrC led to bulging indicative of cell wall defects (Figure 4C, Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C and supplementary figures.

claim: D-alanine rescued biofilm colony growth of alrA monocultures on MSgg-xylose plates.
source: To test this hypothesis, we grew monocultures of an alrA strain without gfp in the genome on MSgg-xylose with exogenous D-alanine and found that D-alanine rescued biofilm colony growth (Figure 4D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: D-methionine rescued alrA growth on MSgg-xylose plates.
source: D-methionine, an amino acid that can substitute for D-alanine in cell wall cross-linking (Cava et al., 2011), also rescued alrA growth on MSgg-xylose plates (Figure 4D), while other D-amino acids that are not incorporated into the cell wall did not rescue colony growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G), suggesting that D-alanine's specific role in peptidoglycan synthesis is rescued.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and supplementary figures, along with a citation.

claim: Other D-amino acids that are not incorporated into the cell wall did not rescue alrA colony growth.
source: D-methionine, an amino acid that can substitute for D-alanine in cell wall cross-linking (Cava et al., 2011), also rescued alrA growth on MSgg-xylose plates (Figure 4D), while other D-amino acids that are not incorporated into the cell wall did not rescue colony growth (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F, G), suggesting that D-alanine's specific role in peptidoglycan synthesis is rescued.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures.

claim: The vast majority of alrA cells died within hours in both liquid monocultures and co-cultures with the parent-RFP strain.
source: The vast majority of alrA cells died within hours in both liquid monocultures and co-cultures with the parent-RFP strain (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The rescue of alrA knockdown cells by D-alanine sharing in co-cultures is specific to growth in a colony.
source: Thus, the rescue of alrA knockdown cells by D-alanine sharing in co-cultures is specific to growth in a colony, presumably due to the close proximity of cells that facilitates D-alanine sharing.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that rescue occurs in colonies but not in liquid cultures.

claim: Matrix-deficient co-culture colonies were smaller than matrix-proficient co-cultures.
source: As expected, matrix-deficient co-culture colonies were smaller than matrix-proficient co-cultures as matrix is necessary for robust biofilm colony growth (Seminara et al., 2012; Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A and a citation.

claim: Matrix-deficient co-cultures exhibited approximately the same fraction of alrA cells as matrix-proficient co-cultures.
source: Nonetheless, matrix-deficient co-cultures exhibited approximately the same fraction of alrA cells as matrix-proficient co-cultures (Figure 5A, B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B and supplementary figures.

claim: Matrix is not required for the growth rescue of alrA-knockdown cells.
source: Thus, matrix is not required for the growth rescue of alrA-knockdown cells.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that rescue occurs in matrix-deficient co-cultures.

claim: Combining the matrix-proficient alrA strain under full knockdown with the matrix-deficient parent-RFP strain resulted in an increased fraction of alrA-depleted cells relative to co-cultures with the matrix-proficient parent-RFP strain.
source: Surprisingly, combining the matrix-proficient and wrinkling-proficient alrA strain under full knockdown with the matrix-deficient (∆epsH ∆tasA) parent-RFP strain resulted in an increased fraction of alrA-depleted cells relative to co-cultures with the matrix-proficient parent-RFP strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data comparing different co-culture combinations.

claim: The competitive fitness of alrA against the matrix-deficient parent was stable at ~1 for 48 hr.
source: Moreover, rather than a steady decrease in competitive fitness over time (Figure 5A,B), the competitive fitness of alrA against the matrix-deficient parent was stable at ~1 for 48 hr.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5A, B.

claim: The matrix-deficient parent-RFP cells restore viability to alrA knockdown cells by providing D-alanine.
source: The matrix-deficient parent-RFP cells restore viability to alrA knockdown cells by providing D-alanine, and in turn alrA knockdown cells enhance growth of the parent-RFP strain by providing extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutualistic interaction observed between the two strains.

claim: alrA knockdown cells enhance growth of the parent-RFP strain by providing extracellular matrix.
source: The matrix-deficient parent-RFP cells restore viability to alrA knockdown cells by providing D-alanine, and in turn alrA knockdown cells enhance growth of the parent-RFP strain by providing extracellular matrix.
evidence: This is inferred from the mutualistic interaction observed between the two strains.

claim: In all matrix-production combinations, the parent-RFP strain had a growth advantage at the edge of the two-dimensional colony and outcompeted the alrA knockdown.
source: Now, in all matrix-production combinations of the sacA::gfp alrA strain under full knockdown and parent-RFP, including matrix-proficient alrA with the matrix-deficient parent, the parent-RFP strain had a growth advantage at the edge of the two-dimensional colony and outcompeted the alrA knockdown (Figure 5C, F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C, F.

claim: The mutualism between alrA under full knockdown and the matrix-deficient parent can be eliminated by removing the ability of the colony to grow in three dimensions.
source: Thus, the mutualism we discovered between alrA under full knockdown and the matrix-deficient parent can be eliminated by removing the ability of the colony to grow in three dimensions.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that mutualism is lost in two-dimensional growth.

claim: Eight other essential gene full knockdowns exhibited a high mutualism score on MSgg-xylose in addition to alrA.
source: On MSgg-xylose, in addition to alrA, eight other essential gene full knockdowns exhibited a high mutualism score (Figure 5E, Figure 5—figure supplement 1E, F, Supplementary file 5).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and supplementary figures.

claim: Knockdowns of racE and menE were candidates for nutrient- and matrix-sharing mutualisms similar to that of alrA.
source: Of these strains, knockdowns of genes encoding the glutamate racemase (racE) and enzymes involved in menaquinone (vitamin K2) synthesis (menE) were candidates for nutrient- and matrix-sharing mutualisms similar to that of alrA.
evidence: This is inferred from the functional roles of these genes and their mutualism scores.

claim: Knockdowns of menC and menD displayed mutualism scores slightly below 0.22.
source: Knockdowns of two other genes in the menaquinone synthesis pathway (menC and menD) displayed mutualism scores slightly below 0.22 (Figure 5E, Supplementary file 5), providing further support for a menaquinone-based mutualism.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E and supplementary files.

claim: Strains depleted of racE, menE, menD, and rnz showed evidence of being outcompeted by parent-RFP, but stably coexisted throughout the entire colony when the parent could not produce matrix.
source: Strains depleted of racE, menE, menD, and rnz showed evidence of being outcompeted by parent-RFP, but stably coexisted throughout the entire colony when the parent could not produce matrix (Figure 5E), further suggesting that matrix-capable mutants promote growth of the matrix-deficient parent strain.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Four non-essential strains exhibited high mutualism scores.
source: In addition, four non-essential strains exhibited high mutualism scores (Figure 5—figure supplement 1F), indicating that the benefits of matrix sharing can extend to genes that are not critical for growth as a monoculture.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1F.

claim: In each case tested (racE, menE, rnz, and hbs full depletions), the knockdown was outcompeted by the parent-RFP strain at the growing edge of the two-dimensional colony.
source: We grew racE, menE, rnz, and hbs full depletions in individual co-cultures with the matrix-deficient parent-RFP between a glass slide and a coverslip. In each case, the knockdown was outcompeted by the parent-RFP strain at the growing edge of the colony (Figure 5F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Matrix-dependent mutualisms generally require growth in a three-dimensional colony.
source: In sum, these data suggest that matrix-dependent mutualisms generally require growth in a three-dimensional colony.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the observation that mutualisms are lost in two-dimensional growth.

claim: D-alanine levels are undetectable in B. subtilis 168 liquid culture supernatants.
source: Despite previous studies showing that D-alanine levels are undetectable in B. subtilis 168 liquid culture supernatants (Lam et al., 2009), we found that D-alanine sharing in a colony can rescue B. subtilis 3610 mutants that cannot synthesize their own D-alanine.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lam et al., 2009.

claim: D-alanine is produced and secreted by wild-type cells at sufficient levels to support growth of the mutant in a colony on biofilm-promoting media.
source: Thus, D-alanine is produced and secreted by wild-type cells at sufficient levels to support growth of the mutant in a colony on biofilm-promoting media.
evidence: This conclusion is drawn from the rescue of alrA mutants in colonies.

claim: Rescue of alrA mutants likely occurs early in biofilm development prior to the period of substantial cell death.
source: Since full knockdown of alrA causes cells to bulge and die in liquid culture within hours (Figure 4C, E), we infer that rescue likely occurs early in biofilm development prior to the period of substantial cell death that is thought to drive wrinkling (Asally et al., 2012), suggesting that rescue is not due to the release of D-alanine by dying cells.
evidence: This is inferred from the timing of cell death and the rescue phenotype, with a citation.

claim: Cell wall synthesis mutants can be supported in native environments through sharing of cell wall components.
source: Regardless, this rescue demonstrates that cell wall synthesis mutants can be supported in native environments through sharing of cell wall components, which could be provided by many other bacterial species in a multispecies community due to the common chemical makeup of peptidoglycan cell walls (Cava et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a generalization drawn from the alrA rescue data, with a citation.

claim: The stable mutualism between the alrA knockdown and a matrix-deficient parent resembles the initial behavior of ∆tasA and ∆epsH mutants grown together as pellicle biofilms on liquid surfaces.
source: The stable mutualism that we discovered between the alrA knockdown and a matrix-deficient parent (Figure 5B) resembles the initial behavior of ∆tasA and ∆epsH mutants grown together as pellicle biofilms on liquid surfaces, in which the pellicle architecture is preserved by cross-complementation for many passages (Dragoš et al., 2018).
evidence: This comparison is made with a citation to Dragoš et al., 2018.

claim: Growth in a biofilm colony can drive genetic diversity.
source: Together, our results demonstrate that growth in a biofilm colony can drive genetic diversity and illustrate the potential for mutualism between nutrient and matrix sharing in native biofilms.
evidence: This is a general conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Mutualisms involving nutrient and matrix sharing may occur during plant root colonization.
source: Such mutualisms may occur during plant root colonization, when the bacterial extracellular matrix is particularly important and may serve to pull nutrients from the root and surrounding soil (Beauregard et al., 2013).
evidence: This is a speculative statement about potential applications, with a citation.
